## Prime number theorem

Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes at most \(x\). We prove
\[
\boxed{\pi(x)\sim \frac{x}{\log x}}.
\]
The proof below uses the **Wiener–Ikehara Tauberian theorem** as a standard external theorem; its proof is not included.

### 1. Encode prime powers

Define the von Mangoldt function by
\[
\Lambda(n)=
\begin{cases}
\log p,&n=p^k\text{ for a prime }p\text{ and }k\ge1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
and set
\[
\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n),\qquad
\vartheta(x)=\sum_{p\le x}\log p.
\]
We will first prove \(\psi(x)\sim x\), then remove the contribution of higher prime powers, and finally recover \(\pi(x)\).

For \(\Re s>1\), absolute convergence and unique factorization give the Euler product
\[
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}
=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}.
\]
Taking its logarithmic derivative gives
\[
F(s):=-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}
=\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}(\log p)p^{-ks}
=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s}.
\]
In particular, \(F\) is the Mellin–Stieltjes transform of the nondecreasing function \(\psi\):
\[
F(s)=\int_{1^-}^{\infty}x^{-s}\,d\psi(x).
\]

### 2. Continue the zeta function to the boundary

For \(\Re s>1\), integration of the counting function \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) gives
\[
\zeta(s)=s\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-s-1}\,dx
=\frac{s}{s-1}-s\int_1^\infty\{x\}x^{-s-1}\,dx.
\]
Because \(0\le\{x\}<1\), the last integral converges locally uniformly for \(\Re s>0\). This formula therefore continues \(\zeta\) meromorphically to that half-plane. Its only pole there is a simple pole at \(s=1\), with residue \(1\).

The Euler product already shows that \(\zeta\) has no zeros for \(\Re s>1\). The essential next step is to exclude zeros on the boundary line.

### 3. Prove that \(\zeta(1+it)\ne0\) for \(t\ne0\)

For real \(\theta\),
\[
3+4\cos\theta+\cos(2\theta)=2(1+\cos\theta)^2\ge0.
\]
For \(\sigma>1\), the absolutely convergent logarithm of the Euler product consequently gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&3\log\zeta(\sigma)
+4\log|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
+\log|\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\\
&\quad=\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}
\frac{p^{-k\sigma}}{k}
\bigl[3+4\cos(kt\log p)+\cos(2kt\log p)\bigr]
\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Exponentiation yields
\[
\zeta(\sigma)^3
|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^4
|\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge1.
\]
Suppose \(\zeta(1+it)=0\) for some \(t\ne0\), with multiplicity \(m\ge1\). As \(\sigma\downarrow1\),
\[
\zeta(\sigma)=O((\sigma-1)^{-1}),\qquad
\zeta(\sigma+it)=O((\sigma-1)^m).
\]
Moreover, \(\zeta(\sigma+2it)\) stays bounded, since \(1+2it\ne1\). Thus the left side of the preceding inequality is
\[
O((\sigma-1)^{4m-3})\longrightarrow0,
\]
contradicting its lower bound of \(1\). Hence the asserted nonvanishing holds.

### 4. Apply the Tauberian theorem

We use the following form of Wiener–Ikehara:

> Let \(A\) be nonnegative, nondecreasing, and right-continuous on \([1,\infty)\). Suppose
> \[
> G(s)=\int_{1^-}^{\infty}x^{-s}\,dA(x)
> \]
> converges for \(\Re s>1\). If, for some \(a\ge0\), the function \(G(s)-a/(s-1)\) extends holomorphically across every point of \(\Re s=1\), then \(A(x)/x\to a\).

We verify its hypotheses with \(A=\psi\), \(G=F\), and \(a=1\).

At every boundary point \(1+it\) with \(t\ne0\), the zeta function is holomorphic and nonzero. Therefore \(-\zeta'/\zeta\) is holomorphic in a neighborhood of that point.

Near \(1\), write
\[
\zeta(s)=\frac{h(s)}{s-1},\qquad h(1)=1,
\]
where \(h\) is holomorphic and nonzero in a sufficiently small neighborhood. Then
\[
-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}
=\frac1{s-1}-\frac{h'(s)}{h(s)}.
\]
Consequently, \(F(s)-1/(s-1)\) is holomorphic near \(1\) as well. All hypotheses hold, so
\[
\boxed{\psi(x)\sim x}.
\]

### 5. Remove higher prime powers

The difference between \(\psi\) and \(\vartheta\) is
\[
0\le\psi(x)-\vartheta(x)
=\sum_{\substack{p^k\le x\\k\ge2}}\log p.
\]
Here \(p\le\sqrt{x}\), and there are at most \(\log x/\log2\) possible exponents. Bounding each summand by \(\log x\) gives
\[
\psi(x)-\vartheta(x)
=O(\sqrt{x}(\log x)^2)=o(x).
\]
Thus
\[
\vartheta(x)\sim x.
\]

### 6. Recover the number of primes

Since \(\log p\le\log x\) for \(p\le x\),
\[
\vartheta(x)\le\pi(x)\log x.
\]
It follows that
\[
\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{\pi(x)\log x}{x}\ge1.
\]
For the reverse bound, fix \(0<\alpha<1\). Each prime in \((x^\alpha,x]\) contributes at least \(\alpha\log x\) to \(\vartheta(x)\), so
\[
\pi(x)\le\pi(x^\alpha)+\frac{\vartheta(x)}{\alpha\log x}
\le x^\alpha+\frac{\vartheta(x)}{\alpha\log x}.
\]
Multiplying by \(\log x/x\), taking the upper limit, and using \(\vartheta(x)/x\to1\), we obtain
\[
\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{\pi(x)\log x}{x}\le\frac1\alpha.
\]
Letting \(\alpha\uparrow1\) proves
\[
\boxed{\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\pi(x)\log x}{x}=1}.
\]
This is the prime number theorem. \(\square\)
